assessment.nobel_worthiness: Combines a task-based framework for technology and labour demand with the quasi-experimental trade-shock evidence on local labour markets. It answers a big question about wages, jobs and inequality, has had wide impact on research and policy, and fits the view that new data plus an explanatory framework together make a contribution.
assessment.attribution: Autor is central to both strands. Katz is central to the skill-biased technical change and education-versus-technology framework. Hanson is central to the trade-shock and regional adjustment work. Dorn is a key co-author of the trade-shock papers and is left out because the prize allows at most three laureates, which is a genuine attribution cost.
assessment.maturity: The foundational work dates from the late 1990s to the 2000s, and the China-shock papers from the 2010s. It has been replicated, extended and debated for years, so the timing is mature.
uncertainties: The China-shock identification and its external validity are still debated.
The three-laureate limit leaves out Dorn and others.
The prize may partly overlap with earlier recognition of labour-economics methods.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The random-coefficients demand estimation framework with endogenous prices (BLP) and the dynamic industry models changed empirical industrial organisation. They are used in antitrust, merger review and regulation, and in many other fields. The contribution is a method that is both rigorous and widely applied.
assessment.attribution: The BLP core is clearly Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes, which maps neatly onto three laureates. Pakes also led the dynamic-games work with Ericson and McGuire. The wider list of names is not credited at the same level for the core demand contribution.
assessment.maturity: BLP dates from 1994 to 1995 and has more than three decades of use and validation, so it is very mature.
uncertainties: The dynamic-industry strand has other important contributors, such as Bresnahan, Benkard, Reiss and Levin.
The computational and identification limits of BLP are known.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Uses population-scale administrative data to measure intergenerational mobility, its geography and the effects of neighbourhoods. It created a new empirical standard on a major question and shaped policy debate. It pairs data discovery with credible quasi-experimental designs, in line with the committee's criteria.
assessment.attribution: Chetty is the clear intellectual leader, with Friedman and Hendren as principal co-authors of the mobility and neighbourhood-effects work. Katz is credited in the longlist, but his core contribution is better placed under the technology and labour-demand candidate.
assessment.maturity: The main papers date from 2014 to 2022. The finding is well replicated across countries, but the long-run causal neighbourhood evidence is still being confirmed.
uncertainties: The work is relatively recent.
Debates continue over causal versus descriptive interpretation and over the mechanisms.
The prize could be seen as better timed in a few years.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Shows with micro data that household leverage and credit supply drive housing booms, consumption drops and recessions. This reshaped macro-finance after the 2008 crisis. It combines new data with an explanatory framework and has significant policy relevance.
assessment.attribution: Mian and Sufi are a tightly paired team behind the core empirical and conceptual findings. Campbell's contributions to household finance and asset pricing are valuable but distinct from this discovery, so I do not propose him.
assessment.maturity: The work dates from roughly 2009 to 2015, with a book and a large follow-up literature. It is reasonably mature, though less seasoned than older candidates.
uncertainties: There is some overlap with earlier financial-crisis and credit-cycle recognition.
Causal interpretation and external validity are still debated.
The case would be stronger with more time.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting changed trade theory and measurement after the new trade theory. The framework explains empirical facts about exporters and gives a new channel for gains from trade. It is conceptually influential and widely used in quantitative work.
assessment.attribution: Melitz (2003) is the key paper. Helpman is credited for heterogeneous-firm extensions, including with Melitz and Yeaple, and for foundational trade theory. Redding is an important contributor to the quantitative strand but is less central to the founding contribution.
assessment.maturity: Dates from 2003 onward and has been extensively tested and extended, so it is mature.
uncertainties: Some credit overlaps with earlier work on trade (Krugman) and with Bernard, Jensen and others on the empirics.
Helpman also appears in a separate candidate, and the best attribution is debatable.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The New Keynesian framework, with Calvo pricing, the Taylor rule and microfounded monetary-policy analysis, underlies modern central-bank practice. It is a major conceptual and policy contribution.
assessment.attribution: Credit is widely dispersed. Woodford and Gali anchor the canonical framework and the policy analysis. Taylor is credited for the policy rule and staggered contracts. Calvo, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler are also important, so any three-laureate selection is contestable and leaves out some important contributors.
assessment.maturity: Developed over four decades, with extensive use in practice, so it is very mature. This also raises the risk that credit is too diffuse to sort cleanly.
uncertainties: The attribution problem is severe.
Post-2008 and post-2021 inflation experience has tested the framework, which is a plus for relevance but a caveat on its fit.
Taylor's stated contribution is more a policy rule than a framework.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Foundations of intertemporal open-economy macroeconomics and the analysis of exchange-rate puzzles. The work is conceptually central to international macro and has shaped policy analysis, though the puzzles remain only partly resolved.
assessment.attribution: Obstfeld and Rogoff are the natural pair, through Foundations of International Macroeconomics and the 'New Open Economy Macroeconomics' papers. Rogoff also appears in a separate candidate, which makes the credit split less clean.
assessment.maturity: Dates from the 1990s, so it is mature, with long exposure to scrutiny.
uncertainties: The exchange-rate disconnect puzzles are not resolved, which weakens the claim of a settled discovery.
Some contributions overlap with earlier recognized work in open-economy macro.
Rogoff's work on crises is not part of this candidate.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Assembled long-run tax-record series on top incomes and wealth, plus measures of offshore wealth. This is tireless archival data work that created a new empirical basis for inequality research and had large intellectual and societal impact, in line with the criteria on data discovery combined with explanation. Political reception is not a consideration.
assessment.attribution: Piketty and Saez built the top-income series, and Zucman extended them to wealth and offshore holdings. Atkinson, who is not credited, was an important predecessor. Saez also appears in the optimal-taxation candidate.
assessment.maturity: The main work dates from 2003 to 2018 and has influenced official statistics. The data are mature, but some of the explanatory claims are still contested.
uncertainties: There are methodological disputes over measurement choices and the wealth-concentration estimates.
The theoretical explanation (the r>g framework) is debated.
It is less clear that the framework, as opposed to the data, merits the prize.
